outcome: No event dated since 26 January 2024 was found that moves the question of whether three unknotted, not-all-circle curves can fail to be arranged into the Borromean rings; the substantive events are older (Cook's conjecture on his web page, dated only to 1998, and Hugh Howards' 2013 journal paper with partial results for polygonal unknots and a conjectured but unproven counterexample), and no later work found engages them.
problem_asks: Written from the bullet's statement alone. (1) Existence: is there a triple of unknotted space curves (each a simple closed curve whose knot type is trivial) that is not three circles, and that cannot be arranged to form the Borromean rings? A 'yes' needs one such triple; a 'no' needs every triple that is unknotted and not all circles to be arrangeable. (2) The exception is exactly 'not all three circles', so at least one component must be non-circular; the bullet does not say what kind of non-circular curve (smooth, polygonal, topological, planar or not). (3) 'Arranged' is not defined. The bullet does not say whether the arrangement may use rigid motions only or may also rescale components. Matthew Cook's version of the conjecture is worded the same way, and Howards (2013, section 3) calls that wording ambiguous on scaling, judging the no-scaling reading 'more likely'. (4) 'This link' is the Borromean rings: three components, each pair unlinked, the three together nontrivial. Wikipedia's January 2024 box words the question as 'Are there three unknotted curves, not all circles, that cannot form the Borromean rings?' and attributes the conjecture to Cook 'without scaling'.

events.what_happened: Matthew Cook's personal Caltech page 'Cook's Borromean Ring Links' states the converse of the circle theorem as a conjecture: 'I conjecture that the converse is also true: Rings are the only thing you can't make Borromean rings out of', i.e. any three simple unknotted closed curves in 3-D can always be arranged into the Borromean rings unless they are all circles. The page gives three proofs that round circles cannot form the rings (proof #1 'probably originally by Mike Friedman', proof #3 'by Conway and myself'). It describes its links as highlights from browsing 'in early 1998' and gives no other date. The page does not say whether arranging may rescale. Page opened.
events.delivers: Conjecture only, for all triples: that any three unknotted 3-D curves not all circles can be arranged to form the Borromean rings. Proves nothing itself beyond recording the circle impossibility, which is the excluded all-circle case.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no triple is shown either arrangeable or not.

checked_by.qualification: Knot theorist; later author of the 2013 JKTR paper on this exact conjecture
checked_by.what_they_did: Engaged with the conjecture: proved partial results (polygonal unknots, with scaling; planar pairs, without) and proposed a contrary conjecture (Conjecture 3.1). This is engagement, not a verification of Cook's conjecture.

events.time_since_posted: about 28 years since the page's stated date (1998); the page is undated beyond that
events.direction: Affirmative: Cook predicts that every such triple can be arranged, so he predicts there is no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Michael H. Freedman and Richard K. Skora, 'Strange actions of groups on spheres', J. Differential Geom. 25 (1987) 75-98. Wikipedia's Borromean rings article (opened) credits them with proving that no Brunnian link can be exactly circular, so at least one component of the Borromean rings must be non-circular; Howards' paper describes the same fact. The paper itself was not opened: its Project Euclid listing appeared in search results only.
events.delivers: Round circles cannot form the Borromean rings: at least one component must be non-circular. This covers only the all-circle case, which the bullet already excludes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The non-circular case is untouched.

checked_by.who: Michael H. Freedman and Richard K. Skora
checked_by.qualification: Topologists; authors of a paper in the peer-reviewed Journal of Differential Geometry
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the circle impossibility, as cited by Wikipedia and Howards.

events.direction: Confirms that the circle exception in Cook's 'unless they are all circles' is needed. Neither for nor against the non-circular case.

events.what_happened: B. Lindström and H.-O. Zetterström, 'Borromean circles are impossible', Amer. Math. Monthly 98 (1991) 340-341. An elementary proof that three flat circles cannot form the Borromean rings, apparently unaware of Freedman and Skora. Cited by Wikipedia (opened). The Monthly article was not opened; the reference data comes from a Springer reference list and blog posts in search results, and one Wikipedia mirror lists Lindström alone as author.
events.delivers: Three flat circles cannot form the Borromean rings. Circles only, so excluded by the bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 1991 (reference data only; the article was not opened)

events.doubts: Wikipedia reports that Gunn and Sullivan (2008) say this argument handles only one particular projection. This was not checked against Gunn and Sullivan.
events.direction: Confirms the circle case is impossible. No bearing on the non-circular case.

events.what_happened: Hugh Howards, 'Convex Brunnian links', J. Knot Theory Ramifications 15 (2006) no. 9, 1131-1140, as listed on Howards' publication page (opened). Per a 2025 paper citing it (Strange, Blair and Klotz, seen in search results), this result shows that the Borromean rings are the only 3-component Brunnian link that can be built from convex components. The 2006 paper itself was not opened, so this rests on that secondary report.
events.delivers: Per the secondary report only: among three-component Brunnian links, only the Borromean rings can be realised with convex components. This is about which link types admit convex realisations, not whether a given triple of unknots forms the rings. Convex planar curves include ellipses, so it is context for the non-circular case but does not decide it.
events.direction: Neighbouring. Its convex-realisability result is consistent with ellipses forming the rings, which is positive for the non-circular case but does not address arbitrary unknots.

events.what_happened: Robert Davis, Hugh Howards, Jonathan Newman and Jason Parsley, 'An infinite family of convex Brunnian links in R^n', arXiv:1101.4863 (v1 25 January 2011, the only version; abstract opened), published Geometriae Dedicata 155:1 (2011) 141-149. They construct explicit three-component convex Brunnian links in R^n for every n >= 3, generalising the Borromean rings to higher dimensions.
events.delivers: Existence of convex three-component Brunnian links in every R^n with n >= 3. A neighbouring problem: it does not address whether a given triple of unknots in R^3 forms the Borromean rings.
events.direction: Neighbouring: existence of convex Brunnian links in higher dimensions. Does not bear on the R^3 non-realisability question.
events.object: Explicit three-component convex Brunnian links in R^n for each n >= 3, generalising the Borromean rings (the constructions themselves were not read).

events.what_happened: Hugh Nelson Howards, 'Forming the Borromean rings out of arbitrary polygonal unknots', J. Knot Theory Ramifications 22 (2013) no. 14, 1350083 (World Scientific DOI 10.1142/S0218216513500831; listing on Howards' page, opened). arXiv:1406.3370 (v1 submitted 12 June 2014, the only version; its comments say the final version appears in JKTR; abstract page opened). The arXiv PDF returned binary data, so the text was read through an HTML rendering (ar5iv) via a summarising fetch, which abridged the quotations. Main results: Theorem 2.5, any three polygonal unknots in R^3 can be moved by rigid motions and scaling of the components into the Borromean rings; Theorem 2.6, if at least two of them are planar, rigid motions alone suffice. The result holds for polygonal unknots arbitrarily close to circles, which exact circles cannot be. Section 1 states Cook's conjecture (Conjecture 1.1) in the words above. Section 3 gives: Conjecture 3.1, 'It is possible to find three unknotted curves, one of which is not a circle that cannot be used to form the Borromean rings' (scaling excluded), which the paper presents as contradicting Cook's conjecture; and Conjecture 3.2, 'Any three planar curves can be used to form the Borromean rings as long as at least one is not a circle' (scaling unstated). Section 3 also calls Cook's wording ambiguous on scaling.
events.revisions: Journal issue 2013 (vol. 22, no. 14). arXiv v1 12 June 2014 is the only arXiv version and posts after the journal issue. The JKTR text was not opened, so any differences between arXiv and journal are unchecked.
events.delivers: For polygonal unknots only. (a) Any three polygonal unknots, including ones arbitrarily close to circles, can be arranged into the Borromean rings by rigid motions plus scaling of the components. (b) If at least two are planar, rigid motions alone suffice. Nothing here for smooth or general unknotted curves; nothing for a polygonal triple with no scaling and at most one planar component. The paper proves neither conjecture in section 3.
events.remains: Whether arbitrary unknotted non-circular triples can be arranged by rigid motions alone (Cook's conjecture, and the bullet's question on the no-scaling reading); whether a non-arrangeable triple exists (Conjecture 3.1); the planar version (Conjecture 3.2); and the scaling-permitted question for non-polygonal curves. If the bullet's 'arranged' allows scaling, (a) answers it for polygonal triples only.

checked_by.who: Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications (World Scientific), refereed
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2013. No referee report is public.

events.time_since_posted: about 12 years since arXiv (June 2014); about 13 years since the 2013 journal issue. No public engagement beyond citations was found; citation coverage was poor (see incomplete).
events.directly_checkable: The theorems are constructive for polygonal input, so a given polygonal triple could be checked by computer, but no such check was made here. The Cantarella candidate below is an explicit curve set whose arrangeability is not settled by the paper.
events.direction: Partial support for Cook's conjecture, in the paper's own words as read in the summary: the affirmative answer for polygonal unknots with scaling, and for planar pairs without it. It proposes a contrary conjecture (3.1) but proves nothing against Cook. The paper does not say it weakens Cook's conjecture to planar curves; Conjecture 3.2 is a separate planar statement.
events.object: No verified object. Section 3 gives a candidate for Conjecture 3.1, credited to Jason Cantarella: two round circles K1 and K2 of radius 10, together with an unknot K3 isotopic on a torus T to an (n,1) torus knot, built from n meridian arcs outside a small neighbourhood of the origin joined by short arcs on T. An example with n = 18 is drawn (the summaries give 'Figure 9' in one place and 'Figure 10' in another; unresolved). The paper says the example is 'likely to satisfy' Conjecture 3.1 and 'might be a counter-example' to Cook's conjecture if scaling is excluded. It says that if scaling is allowed the example is not a counterexample, since scaling K3 up exposes its non-circular arcs. The paper does not prove that this triple cannot be arranged. It is an explicit, unproven candidate.

events.what_happened: Jonathan Strange, Ryan Blair and Alexander R. Klotz, 'Efficient Detection of Borromean Linking in Ellipses', arXiv:2509.15104 (v1 18 September 2025; abstract page opened; full text not opened). The method counts intersections of one ellipse with the plane of another, after a transformation that sends one ellipse to the unit circle. It decides Hopf linking of two ellipses and Borromean linking of three ellipses. The page does not mention unknotted non-circular curves, Cook's conjecture or Howards' conjectures.
events.delivers: A test for whether three given ellipses form Borromean linking. Restricted to ellipses, which are convex planar curves. It does not show whether any triple of non-circular unknots can be arranged into the rings, so it does not answer the existence question.
events.time_since_posted: about 1 year (preprint; no peer review visible)
events.direction: Neighbouring. Consistent with ellipses forming the rings, which is known from earlier work.

events.what_happened: Alexander Klotz, 'Geometric considerations for energy minimization of topological links and chainmail networks', arXiv:2507.20903 (v1 28 July 2025, the only version; abstract page opened, paraphrased). It studies Möbius and minimum-distance energy minimisers for links including Hopf links and Borromean rings. A search snippet (not verified in the text) reports that three congruent ellipses with mutually orthogonal normals and common centres form the Borromean rings, with minimal energy at aspect ratio about 1.71, and that stadia do slightly better. The abstract does not mention Cook's or Howards' conjectures or unknotted non-circular curves.
events.delivers: Energy-minimising configurations for the Borromean rings built from ellipses and stadia (per the snippet). These are optimisation results for specific curve families, not a classification of which triples can form the rings.
events.time_since_posted: about 1 year (preprint; no peer review visible)
events.doubts: The search tool flagged the snippets describing this paper as partly garbled, so the numerical claims (1.71, 1.78, the 0.5% figure) were not checked against the paper text.
events.direction: Neighbouring. Ellipse configurations, which are known, not a new non-realisable object.
events.object: Per the snippet only: three congruent ellipses with mutually orthogonal normals and common centres forming the Borromean rings. This is a positive realisation of a known type.

Vesnin, 'On a family of hyperbolic Brunnian links and their volumes', arXiv:2503.17974 (v1 23 March 2025; metadata from the arXiv listing and Crossref opened, abstract not opened). Published as chapter 21 of Essays on Topology (Springer, 2025; Crossref online date 22 July 2025, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-81414-3_21).
events.revisions: v1 in the arXiv listing; published as a book chapter in 2025.
events.delivers: Hyperbolic Brunnian links and their volumes. Not about realisation by unknotted curves. Settles nothing here.

checked_by.qualification: Published in a peer-reviewed edited volume (review process not verified)

events.direction: Neighbouring. Brunnian links in a different sense (hyperbolic volumes).

events.what_happened: Seungwon Kim, Gheehyun Nahm and Alison Tatsuoka, 'Brunnian links of 3-balls in the 4-sphere', arXiv:2603.06554 (v1 6 March 2026). Metadata and a one-line description came from a search summary; the abstract page was not opened.
events.delivers: Infinitely many n-component Brunnian links of 3-balls in S^4 for each n >= 2 (per the summary). Higher-dimensional and about 3-balls, not curves in R^3. Settles nothing here.
events.direction: Neighbouring. Brunnian construction in a different setting.

events.what_happened: Boris Botvinnik and Tadayuki Watanabe, 'Brunnian links and Kontsevich graph complex I', arXiv:2601.08200 (v1 13 January 2026). Metadata and a one-line description came from a search summary (a chain map from the Kontsevich graph complex to rational chains on a diffeomorphism space); the abstract page was not opened.

events.what_happened: Luis Celso Chan Palomo and Scott A. Taylor, 'Hyperbolic Brunnian theta curves', arXiv:2512.14533 (v1 16 December 2025). Metadata from the arXiv listing and a search summary; the abstract page was not opened. The objects are theta-graphs in S^3, not three-component links.
events.delivers: Hyperbolic Brunnian theta curves in S^3 (per the summary). A different object from the Borromean rings. Settles nothing here.

events.what_happened: Jean-Yves Degos, 'On the Brunnian conjecture', arXiv:2410.16931 (v1 22 October 2024, the only version; abstract opened). This is a namesake: the Brunnian conjecture here asks whether GL(n,p) is generated by conjugates of companion matrices over a finite field. The paper proves it for p >= 5 when n is not divisible by p-1. It has nothing to do with links.
events.delivers: A result on a different problem that shares the name 'Brunnian conjecture'. Does not bear on the Borromean rings bullet.

events.what_happened: Alexander R. Klotz, 'Borromean Hypergraph Formation in Dense Random Rectangles', arXiv:2405.20874 (v1 31 May 2024). Metadata from the arXiv listing and a search snippet; the abstract was not opened. A polymer-physics simulation of rings forming Borromean links in dense random solutions. It is a namesake: the question is statistical, not about realising the link by unknotted curves.
events.delivers: Statistics on Borromean link formation by random rings in a polymer model. Not a realisability result. Settles nothing here.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different problem that shares the name.

events.what_happened: Anton A. Nazarenko and A. V. Nazarenko, 'Structures associated with the Borromean rings complement in the Poincaré ball', arXiv:2404.02615 (v1 3 April 2024; abstract page opened, paraphrased). It studies the complement's geometry, its fundamental group as isometries, random walks, a Teichmüller space and sine-Gordon structures. Published in Ukrainian Journal of Physics (Crossref date 27 August 2024, DOI 10.15407/ujpe69.7.498).
events.revisions: v1 in the arXiv listing; published Ukrainian Journal of Physics, August 2024 (version history not checked).
events.delivers: Geometry of the Borromean rings complement. Says nothing about realisation of the link by curves. Settles nothing here.

events.what_happened: Shannon Cheng, Anna Chlopecki, Saarah Nazar and Eric Samperton, 'An elementary proof that linking problems are hard', arXiv:2509.13120 (v1 16 September 2025; abstract page opened). It gives an NP-hardness proof for the Trivial Sublink problem by reduction from Independent Set. The authors say the reduction 'allows us to avoid the use of Brunnian links such as the Borromean rings'.
events.delivers: NP-hardness of finding trivial sublinks in link diagrams, using reductions that avoid Borromean rings. Not a realisability result.
events.direction: Not applicable to the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Kristen Hendricks, Matthew Stoffregen and Ian Zemke, 'Link Floer homology, nonformality, and the Borromean rings', arXiv:2608.25295 (v1 26 August 2026; abstract page opened). It computes the full link Floer complex of the Borromean rings, shows that this complex is not a free resolution of its homology, and gives a criterion for formality of L-space links.
events.delivers: The link Floer complex of the Borromean rings. Invariant-theoretic; not about arrangements of unknots. Settles nothing here.
events.direction: Not applicable to the bullet's question.

Metadata from the arXiv listing only; the abstract was not opened. A namesake in physics: the 'Borromean rings' here label a braiding process in a topological field theory.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia's Borromean rings article says Matthew Cook conjectured that the rings can be formed 'without scaling' and that Howards 'weakened the conjecture to apply to any three planar curves that are not all circles'. Cook's own page has no scaling clause. Howards' section 3 calls Cook's wording ambiguous on scaling and judges the no-scaling reading 'more likely', and it does not say Howards weakened Cook's conjecture. Howards' Conjecture 3.2 is a separate planar statement with scaling unstated, and his Conjecture 3.1 contradicts Cook's conjecture on the no-scaling reading. The Wikipedia wording is a reasonable reading of the planar statement, but the paper does not describe it as a weakening.

Circle impossibility, which is background rather than the open question: Freedman and Skora (1987) are credited with proving that at least one component must be non-circular. Lindström and Zetterström (1991) gave a separate proof, apparently unaware of the earlier result. Cook's page attributes its proof #1 to Mike Friedman. A 1995 Usenet post by Mess (quoted on the Geometry Junkyard page) says 'I think the argument is Freedman's'. The attributions differ, but none bears on the non-circular question.

summary: Every event I found is older than the window or is a neighbouring or namesake paper. The problem's canonical wording is in Wikipedia's list (Euclidean geometry, linking to the Borromean rings article), and the Borromean rings article carries an 'Unsolved problem in mathematics' box with the same question, attributed to Matthew Cook's conjecture and to Hugh Howards' follow-up. Cook's conjecture is on his Caltech page (opened), dated only to 'early 1998'. Howards' 2013 JKTR paper (listed on his page, opened) and its arXiv version 1406.3370 (only version, 12 June 2014; abstract opened; PDF unreadable, so the text came through an HTML rendering summarised by a fetch tool, with abridged quotations) proves that any three polygonal unknots can be arranged into the Borromean rings with rigid motions plus scaling, and without scaling when at least two are planar. Section 3 poses Conjecture 3.1 (a non-arrangeable triple with one non-circular curve, no scaling), which is a contrary conjecture, and Conjecture 3.2 (planar triples). The only counterexample candidate is Cantarella's torus construction, which the paper calls 'likely' and 'might be' a counterexample if scaling is excluded; the paper does not prove it. Close call one: whether Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 'settle' anything depends on whether the bullet's 'arranged' allows scaling. With scaling, every polygonal triple is arrangeable, which answers the bullet's question for polygons in the 'no' direction, though the statement is about arbitrary unknotted curves. Without scaling, the theorems cover only polygonal triples with at least two planar members. Close call two: the candidate, if scaling is excluded, would answer 'yes', but the paper gives no proof it fails to arrange, and the paper's own remark that scaling defeats it suggests the no-scaling reading is the one that matters. None of the 2024–2026 arXiv papers with 'Borromean' or 'Brunnian' in the title or abstract that I could list bears on realisation by unknotted curves: they cover ellipse detection and energy minimisation (Strange, Blair and Klotz 2025; Klotz 2025), hyperbolic Brunnian links, Brunnian theta curves, link Floer homology, NP-hardness of trivial sublinks, polymer and physics namesakes, and a Brunnian group-theory conjecture of the same name. The AI search found nothing: none of the searches linked any AI system or AI-generated result to this problem, and no source names a system. The AI-related results I saw (OpenAI's unit-distance disproof, claimed GPT-5 Erdős results, a reported GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra proof, KnotBench, Harmonic's Aristotle) concern other problems or are benchmarks; they were seen in snippets and not opened. Attribution of the circle impossibility is contested, but it is background that the bullet excludes.
competing_reading: The strongest reading against 'nothing has moved' is that Howards' Theorem 2.5 and 2.6 are substantive progress on exactly this question. If the bullet's 'arranged' includes rescaling (which Wikipedia's 'without scaling' reading does not), the theorems settle the question for every polygonal triple, leaving only non-polygonal curves open. On that reading the question is largely answered in the 'no counterexample' direction, and the Cantarella candidate becomes irrelevant. The strongest reading the other way is that Cantarella's torus triple is already a counterexample under the no-scaling reading. The paper says it is 'likely' and 'might be' one, and its scaling discussion makes the no-scaling reading the one that matters. On that reading the answer is 'yes' once the candidate is verified. Both readings depend on the paper's exact wording, which I read only through a summarising fetch.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A proof, or a verified computation, that Cantarella's torus triple (or any triple of unknotted non-circular curves) cannot be arranged into the Borromean rings by rigid motions alone; this answers 'yes' on the no-scaling reading. (2) A proof that every triple of unknotted curves not all circles can be arranged by rigid motions alone, which answers 'no' (Cook's conjecture). (3) Clarification of 'arranged' in the bullet's source; this decides whether Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 already answer the question for polygons. (4) The JKTR text of section 3, checked against the arXiv PDF, to confirm the exact wording of Conjectures 1.1, 3.1 and 3.2, and whether the published version differs. (5) MathSciNet or zbMATH reviews, or citing papers from 2014 onward, that engage Conjectures 1.1, 3.1 or 3.2. (6) The reference behind the Wikipedia list's note [75] and the Wikipedia box's undated source.

judgement.why: The only event that settles any part of the statement is Howards' 2013 JKTR paper: it shows every polygonal triple with at least two planar members can be arranged by rigid motions alone (and every polygonal triple with scaling), so within a restricted class there is no counterexample. That is a case, peer-reviewed, and pre-snapshot; it is not whole because the statement covers arbitrary unknotted curves and the scaling reading is unclear. The Cantarella torus triple is only a conjectured candidate with no proof, so it is no counterexample object. The circle impossibility results (Freedman-Skora, Lindström-Zetterström) concern the case the statement excludes and are background, scored none. Cook's page is a conjecture, none. All 2024-2026 events are either ellipse-specific detection/energy work that does not decide the existence question (none) or different questions and namesakes (variant). No AI involvement anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Howards' text was read only through a summarising fetch; exact wording of Theorems 2.5/2.6 and Conjectures 3.1/3.2 unverified. Citation coverage after 2014 was poor, so later engagement with Howards' conjectures could exist unseen.
